source.title: Infraslow histaminergic dynamics govern priming states to gate moment-to-moment memory accessibility

confidence_rationale: This is the founding paper for MECH-425 Line A -- the causal, bidirectional demonstration that a global, slowly-fluctuating, arousal-coupled signal (TMN histamine) sets moment-to-moment retrieval readiness. It strongly grounds that Line A is a REAL, content-blind reinstatement-gain knob. But it addresses only ONE of Q-076's two factors: it demonstrates the gain layer and its main effect, not the interaction with a content-selective suppression operator (Line B). Confidence is therefore moderate and partial -- high-quality evidence for a component of Q-076, not for its interaction claim.
failure_signatures: The histaminergic gain demonstrated here is content-BLIND -- it uniformly scales cue-evoked BLA responses and memory expression -- which is exactly Q-076's Line-A main effect (high gain without selective suppression -> the problematic-interference corner). The paper shows the gain exists but not that it is managed by a competitor-selective suppression arm, so on its own it cannot establish the interaction Q-076 predicts.

Effect is on reward-associative Pavlovian memory read out via a single behavioural expression measure in mice; it does not score competing co-encoded traces individually, so interference vs correct-trace reinstatement cannot be dissociated within this dataset.

mapping.source_claim_statement: Spontaneous pre-cue activity of TMN histaminergic neurons shows infraslow (0.05-0.1 Hz) dynamics tracking an integrated brain-body state; high-histaminergic states enhance memory expression, and brief optogenetic activation/inhibition before the cue bidirectionally modulates expression by priming BLA circuits for robust cue responses.
mapping.ree_translation: MECH-425 Line A posits a global, slowly-fluctuating, arousal-coupled reinstatement-gain layer on retrieval. Morishita et al. provide the causal biological instantiation: an infraslow histaminergic state variable that sets, moment to moment, how strongly a fixed cue reinstates its associated memory. Q-076 asks whether this gain, crossed with a content-selective suppression operator, governs the interference-vs-forgetting tradeoff; this paper anchors the gain factor as real and causal.
mapping.mapping_caveat: Grounds ONLY Line A. The gain here is global and content-blind (it scales the whole cue-evoked response), so it speaks to Q-076's Line-A main-effect prediction (uniform reinstatement change = apparent forgetting when clamped low; unmanaged access when high) but says nothing about the Line-B selective-suppression arm or the interaction term that Q-076 actually turns on. Mouse reward-associative memory in BLA, not human episodic/ContextMemory readout.
mapping.source_context: In vivo mouse; fibre photometry of TMN histaminergic neurons, closed-loop cue delivery, optogenetic activation/inhibition, BLA population recording; Pavlovian reward-associative memory.

confidence_components.notes: Source quality high (Neuron; causal, bidirectional, closed-loop optogenetics with a circuit mechanism). Mapping fidelity 0.52: excellent for Line A alone, but Q-076 is an INTERACTION question and this paper supplies only one factor. Transfer risk moderate: mouse Pavlovian BLA memory -> REE read-time policy over episodic/ContextMemory is a real species/system gap, and the histaminergic gain being content-blind is precisely the corner Q-076 warns must be paired with selective suppression.
